questions.q: What are PostgreSQL's two common equivalents for T-SQL's IDENTITY(1,1)?
options: SEQUENCE_KEY and ROWID, both PostgreSQL-only keywords
PostgreSQL has no way to auto-increment a primary key
GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (modern, standard) and SERIAL (older, PostgreSQL-specific shortcut)
AUTO_INCREMENT and IDENTITY, identical to MySQL and T-SQL respectively
questions.explain: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the modern, standard-compliant choice; SERIAL is the older PostgreSQL-specific shortcut still common in existing code.

questions.q: Where does PostgreSQL's LIMIT clause go, compared to T-SQL's TOP?
options: LIMIT must be the very first keyword in the statement
LIMIT goes at the end of the query; TOP goes right after SELECT
LIMIT goes immediately after SELECT, exactly where TOP does
LIMIT goes before the FROM clause
questions.explain: Same structural move as the MySQL translation in Chapter 7 — LIMIT belongs at the end, not right after SELECT.

questions.q: What replaces T-SQL's ISNULL function in PostgreSQL?
options: ISNULL works identically in PostgreSQL
COALESCE — PostgreSQL has no ISNULL function at all
IFNULL, borrowed directly from MySQL syntax
NVL, borrowed directly from Oracle syntax
questions.explain: PostgreSQL has no ISNULL function; COALESCE is the standard, portable replacement used across every dialect in this course.

questions.q: Which parts of the example query needed zero changes when translating from T-SQL to PostgreSQL?
options: Only the table name needed to change
Every single clause needed to be rewritten from scratch
The WHERE clause was the only part that needed changing
SELECT, FROM, ORDER BY, and the column list — only IDENTITY, TOP, and ISNULL needed replacement
questions.explain: This reinforces the chapter's recurring theme: most of a query's structure is portable; only a handful of vendor-specific pieces need translation.

questions.q: Why is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY described as the better choice for new PostgreSQL code over SERIAL?
options: SERIAL has been completely removed from PostgreSQL and no longer works
It's the modern, standard-SQL-compliant syntax, while SERIAL is an older PostgreSQL-specific shortcut
GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is faster at insert time in every case
SERIAL only works for TEXT columns, not INT columns
questions.explain: Both still work, but GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY aligns with the SQL standard, while SERIAL is a PostgreSQL-specific convenience from before that standard existed.
